problem.summary: 如何利用CLIP等对比模型学习到的鲁棒图像表示（同时捕获语义和风格）来改进文本条件图像生成，以提升生成图像的多样性和质量。

motivation.summary: CLIP嵌入具有鲁棒性、零样本能力和优秀的语义-风格表示。扩散模型在图像生成方面表现优异。将两者结合，利用CLIP表示来指导生成，有望在保持照片真实感的同时显著提升生成多样性。

core_idea.summary: 提出一个两阶段模型（unCLIP）：1）先验模型（Prior）根据文本描述生成CLIP图像嵌入；2）解码器（Decoder）根据该图像嵌入生成最终图像。通过显式生成图像表示，可以提升多样性，并支持图像变体、插值和语言引导的编辑等操作。

method.summary: 1. 解码器：基于扩散模型（修改自GLIDE），通过投影和添加CLIP嵌入来条件化。2. 先验模型：探索了自回归（AR）和扩散（Diffusion）两种模型，将文本描述映射到CLIP图像嵌入。扩散先验在计算效率和样本质量上更优。3. 训练：CLIP模型在训练先验和解码器时保持冻结。

experiments.summary: 在MS-COCO数据集上进行零样本FID评估，与DALL-E、GLIDE等模型对比。进行人类评估（照片真实感、描述相似性、多样性）。进行美学质量评估。展示图像变体、插值和文本差异编辑等定性结果。

claims.claim: 显式生成图像表示（CLIP嵌入）可以提升生成图像的多样性，同时保持照片真实感和描述相似性。
基于CLIP嵌入条件化的解码器可以生成保留语义和风格的图像变体。
CLIP的联合嵌入空间支持零样本的语言引导图像编辑。
扩散先验比自回归先验计算效率更高，且能产生更高质量的样本。
unCLIP在MS-COCO零样本FID上达到了新的最优水平（10.39）。
与GLIDE相比，unCLIP在引导下能更好地保持多样性。

limitations.limitation: 在将属性绑定到对象方面比GLIDE更差（例如，难以区分两个不同颜色的立方体）。
难以生成连贯的文本（例如，拼写错误）。
在复杂场景中生成细节的能力有限。
CLIP嵌入本身可能不显式编码对象-属性绑定或精确的文本拼写信息。
存在潜在风险，如生成图像被误认为真实图像，以及模型可能学习训练数据中的偏见。

nodes.title: CLIP模型
nodes.label: 表示学习器
nodes.summary: CLIP是一个对比模型，学习图像和文本的联合嵌入空间，其图像嵌入捕获语义和风格信息。
nodes.description: CLIP模型在训练过程中学习一个联合表示空间，用于图像和文本。在unCLIP的训练中，CLIP模型是冻结的，仅用于提取图像和文本嵌入。

nodes.title: 先验模型
nodes.label: 文本到嵌入映射
nodes.summary: 先验模型根据文本描述生成CLIP图像嵌入。探索了自回归和扩散两种实现。
nodes.description: 先验模型P(zi|y)接收文本描述y，输出CLIP图像嵌入zi。自回归先验将嵌入离散化后自回归预测；扩散先验直接建模连续向量。扩散先验更高效且质量更高。

nodes.title: 解码器
nodes.label: 嵌入到图像生成
nodes.summary: 解码器是一个扩散模型，根据CLIP图像嵌入（可选文本描述）生成图像。
nodes.description: 解码器P(x|zi, y)基于CLIP图像嵌入zi和可选文本y生成图像x。它修改自GLIDE架构，通过投影和添加CLIP嵌入来条件化。训练时随机丢弃CLIP嵌入以支持无分类器引导。

nodes.title: 图像变体生成
nodes.label: 图像编辑操作
nodes.summary: 通过编码图像到CLIP嵌入和DDIM潜码，然后解码（添加随机性）来生成语义和风格相似的变体。
nodes.description: 给定图像x，编码得到CLIP图像嵌入zi和DDIM潜码xT。解码时使用η>0的DDIM采样引入随机性，生成保留zi信息的变体。

nodes.title: 图像插值
nodes.label: 图像编辑操作
nodes.summary: 通过球面插值两个图像的CLIP嵌入，并解码插值结果，来生成混合两个图像概念的图像。
nodes.description: 对两个图像的CLIP嵌入zi1和zi2进行球面插值，得到ziθ。解码时可以插值DDIM潜码或固定随机潜码。

nodes.title: 文本差异编辑
nodes.label: 图像编辑操作
nodes.summary: 通过计算目标文本和当前描述文本嵌入的差异向量，并将其与图像嵌入插值，实现语言引导的图像编辑。
nodes.description: 计算文本差异向量zd = norm(zt - zt0)。将图像嵌入zi与zd进行球面插值，得到zθ，然后解码。这允许零样本的语言引导图像操作。

nodes.title: 无分类器引导
nodes.label: 采样技术
nodes.summary: 在训练时随机丢弃条件信息（文本或CLIP嵌入），在采样时通过引导尺度增强条件效果，提升样本质量。
nodes.description: 在训练先验和解码器时，随机丢弃条件信息（如10%或5%的时间）。采样时，通过引导尺度调整条件和无条件预测的混合，以提升质量。

deltas.before: GLIDE直接根据文本描述生成图像，所有语义信息都通过文本编码器传递。
deltas.after: unCLIP首先通过先验模型将文本映射到CLIP图像嵌入空间，然后解码器根据该嵌入生成图像。语义信息通过CLIP嵌入传递。
deltas.why_it_matters: 显式生成图像表示（CLIP嵌入）允许模型在生成前固定语义信息，从而在提升引导尺度时保持多样性，而GLIDE的多样性会随引导尺度增加而下降。此外，CLIP嵌入支持图像变体、插值和文本差异编辑等额外操作。

deltas.before: GLIDE等模型通常使用单一的文本条件路径。
deltas.after: unCLIP的解码器同时使用CLIP图像嵌入和可选的文本描述进行条件化。训练时随机丢弃CLIP嵌入以支持无分类器引导。
deltas.why_it_matters: 这种设计允许解码器学习CLIP可能未捕获的自然语言方面（如变量绑定），同时通过无分类器引导提升样本质量。实验发现，同时使用两者效果最佳。

deltas.before: 先前的文本到图像模型（如DALL-E）可能使用自回归先验。
deltas.after: unCLIP探索了自回归和扩散两种先验模型，并发现扩散先验在计算效率和样本质量上更优。
deltas.why_it_matters: 扩散先验直接建模连续的CLIP嵌入，避免了自回归先验所需的离散化步骤，从而更高效且质量更高。

deltas.before: 传统图像生成模型通常只能进行文本到图像的生成。
deltas.after: unCLIP通过编码-解码框架，支持图像变体、插值和语言引导的编辑等多种操作。
deltas.why_it_matters: 这扩展了模型的应用范围，使其不仅能生成图像，还能理解和操作现有图像的语义和风格。

formulas.latex: P(x|y) = P(x, z_i|y) = P(x|z_i, y) P(z_i|y)
formulas.intuition: 这是unCLIP的核心生成过程分解。它表明，要从文本y生成图像x，可以先通过先验模型生成CLIP图像嵌入z_i，再通过解码器根据z_i生成图像x。这利用了链式法则和z_i是x的确定性函数这一事实。

formulas.latex: L_{\text{prior}} = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim [1,T], z_i^{(t)} \sim q_t} \left[ \| f_\theta(z_i^{(t)}, t, y) - z_i \|^2 \right]

variables.name: z_i^{(t)}
variables.description: 在时间步t的加噪CLIP图像嵌入

variables.name: f_\theta
variables.description: 去噪网络（预测干净嵌入）

formulas.intuition: 这是扩散先验的训练目标。它通过最小化去噪网络预测的干净嵌入与真实干净嵌入之间的均方误差来训练先验模型。这类似于标准的扩散模型训练，但目标是在嵌入空间而非像素空间。
这是文本差异编辑的核心公式。通过将原始图像嵌入z_i与文本差异向量z_d进行球面插值，得到编辑后的嵌入z_i^θ。解码该嵌入即可实现语言引导的图像编辑。

main_result.description: 在MS-COCO验证集上评估零样本FID，与DALL-E、GLIDE等模型对比。
main_result.result: unCLIP（扩散先验）达到FID 10.39，优于GLIDE（12.24）和其他模型，成为新的最优水平。

main_result.experiment: 人类评估（照片真实感、描述相似性、多样性）
main_result.description: 人类评估员比较unCLIP和GLIDE生成的图像。
main_result.result: unCLIP在多样性上显著优于GLIDE（扩散先验：70.5%），在照片真实感和描述相似性上与GLIDE相当或略优。

ablation.experiment: 先验模型类型比较（AR vs Diffusion）
ablation.description: 比较自回归先验和扩散先验的性能。
ablation.result: 扩散先验在FID和人类评估（照片真实感、描述相似性、多样性）上均优于自回归先验。

ablation.experiment: 解码器条件化方式比较
ablation.description: 比较解码器仅使用文本、使用文本+CLIP文本嵌入、使用文本+CLIP图像嵌入（来自先验）的效果。
ablation.result: 使用文本+CLIP图像嵌入（unCLIP方式）效果最好（FID 7.99），优于仅使用文本（FID 9.16）和使用文本+CLIP文本嵌入（FID 16.55）。

robustness.experiment: 引导尺度对多样性的影响
robustness.description: 研究增加引导尺度对GLIDE和unCLIP生成多样性的影响。
robustness.result: GLIDE的多样性随引导尺度增加而显著下降，而unCLIP的多样性下降较少，因为语义信息已固定在CLIP嵌入中。

scaling.description: 论文中使用的模型规模信息。
scaling.result: 解码器为3.5B参数的GLIDE模型，先验模型为1B参数，CLIP模型为ViT-H/16。具体超参数见附录。

case_study.experiment: 图像变体、插值和文本差异编辑的定性展示
case_study.description: 展示unCLIP支持的各种图像操作能力。
case_study.result: 成功展示了保留语义和风格的图像变体、混合两个图像概念的插值、以及语言引导的编辑（如将猫变成超级赛亚人猫）。

case_study.description: 通过PCA降维和重建来探索CLIP嵌入空间的结构。
case_study.result: 低维PCA保留粗粒度语义信息，高维PCA编码更精细的细节。这有助于理解CLIP嵌入捕获的信息。

human_eval.experiment: 照片真实感、描述相似性、多样性的成对比较
human_eval.description: 人类评估员在unCLIP和GLIDE生成的图像对之间进行选择。
human_eval.result: unCLIP在多样性上显著胜出，在照片真实感和描述相似性上与GLIDE相当。

human_eval.description: 使用CLIP线性探针预测美学评分，比较unCLIP和GLIDE在艺术提示上的表现。
human_eval.result: unCLIP在美学质量上与GLIDE相当或更优，且引导不会降低召回率。

metadata.paper_type: Computer Vision / Pose Estimation / Vision-Language / Captioning / Computer Vision / Diffusion / Computer Vision / Contrastive Learning / Computer Vision / Top-cited Computer Vision paper
metadata.abstract: Contrastive models like CLIP have been shown to learn robust representations of images that capture both semantics and style. To leverage these representations for image generation, we propose a two-stage model: a prior that generates a CLIP image embedding given a text caption, and a decoder that generates an image conditioned on the image embedding. We show that explicitly generating image representations improves image diversity with minimal loss in photorealism and caption similarity. Our decoders conditioned on image representations can also produce variations of an image that preserve both its semantics and style, while varying the non-essential details absent from the image representation. Moreover, the joint embedding space of CLIP enables language-guided image manipulations in a zero-shot fashion. We use diffusion models for the decoder and experiment with both autoregressive and diffusion models for the prior, finding that the latter are computationally more efficient and produce higher-quality samples.

anchors.text_span: Hierarchical Text-Conditional Image Generation with CLIP Latents Aditya Ramesh∗ OpenAI aramesh@openai.com Prafulla Dhariwal∗ OpenAI prafulla@openai.com Alex Nichol∗ OpenAI alex@openai.com Casey Chu∗ OpenAI casey@openai.com Mark Chen OpenAI mark@openai.com
Abstract

Contrastive models like CLIP have been shown to learn robust representations of images that capture both semantics and style. To leverage these representations for image generation, we propose a two-stage model: a prior that generates a CLIP image embedding given a text caption, and a decoder that generates an image conditioned on the image embedding. We show that explicitly generating image
representations improves image diversity with minimal loss in photorealism and

caption similarity. Our decoders conditioned on image representations can also produce variations of an image that preserve both its semantics and style, while varying the non-essential details absent from the image representation. Moreover, the joint embedding space of CLIP enables language-guided image manipulations in a zero-shot fashion. We use diffusion models for the decoder and experiment with both autoregressive and diffusion models for the prior, ﬁnding that the latter are computationally more efﬁcient and produce higher-quality samples.
1 Introduction
Recent progress in computer vision has been driven by scaling models on large datasets of captioned

images collected from the internet [10, 44, 60, 39, 31, 16]. Within this framework, CLIP [39] has emerged as a successful representation learner for images. CLIP embeddings have a number of desirable properties: they are robust to image distribution shift, have impressive zero-shot capabilities, and have been ﬁne-tuned to achieve state-of-the-art results on a wide variety of vision and language tasks [45]. Concurrently, diffusion models [ 46, 48, 25] have emerged as a promising generative modeling framework, pushing the state-of-the-art on image and video generation tasks [11, 26, 24]. To achieve best results, diffusion models leverage a guidance technique [ 11, 24] which improves sample ﬁdelity (for images, photorealism) at the cost of sample diversity. In this work, we combine these two approaches for the problem of text-conditional image generation.
We ﬁrst train a diffusiondecoder to invert the CLIP image encoder. Our inverter is non-deterministic,

and can produce multiple images corresponding to a given image embedding. The presence of an encoder and its approximate inverse (the decoder) allows for capabilities beyond text-to-image translation. As in GAN inversion [62, 55], encoding and decoding an input image produces semanti- cally similar output images (Figure 3). We can also interpolate between input images by inverting interpolations of their image embeddings (Figure 4). To obtain a full generative model of images, we combine the CLIP image embeddingdecoder with a prior model, which generates possible CLIP image embeddings from a given text caption. We compare our text-to-image system with other systems such as DALL-E [40] and GLIDE [35], ﬁnding that our samples are comparable in quality to GLIDE, but with greater diversity in our generations. We also develop methods for training diffusion priors in latent space, and show that they achieve comparable performance to autoregressive priors, while being more compute-efﬁcient. We refer to our full text-conditional image generation stack as unCLIP, since it generates images by inverting the CLIP image encoder.
2 Method

Our training dataset consists of pairs (x,y ) of imagesx and their corresponding captionsy. Given an imagex, letzi andzt be its CLIP image and text embeddings, respectively. We design our generative stack to produce images from captions using two components: • A priorP (zi|y) that produces CLIP image embeddingszi conditioned on captionsy. • A decoder P (x|zi,y ) that produces images x conditioned on CLIP image embeddings zi (and optionally text captionsy). The decoder allows us to invert images given their CLIP image embeddings, while the prior allows us to learn a generative model of the image embeddings themselves. Stacking these two components yields a generative modelP (x|y) of imagesx given captionsy:
P (x|y) = P (x,zi|y) = P (x|zi,y )P (zi|y).
The ﬁrst equality holds becausezi is a deterministic function ofx. The second equality holds because of the
chain rule. Thus, we can sample from the true conditional distributionP (x|y) by ﬁrst samplingzi using the 3
prior, and then samplingx using the decoder. In the following sections, we describe our decoder and prior stacks. For training details and hyperparameters, refer to Appendix C.
2.1 Decoder

We use diffusion models [25, 48] to produce images conditioned on CLIP image embeddings (and optionally text captions). Speciﬁcally, we modify the architecture described in Nichol et al. (2021) by projecting and adding CLIP embeddings to the existing timestep embedding, and by projecting CLIP embeddings into four extra tokens of context that are concatenated to the sequence of outputs from the GLIDE text encoder. We retained the text conditioning pathway present in the original GLIDE model, hypothesizing that it could allow the diffusion model to learn aspects of natural language that CLIP fails to capture (e.g. variable binding), but ﬁnd that it offers little help in this regard (Section 7). While we can sample from the conditional distribution of the decoder directly, past work using diffusion models shows using guidance on the conditioning information [11, 24, 35] improves sample quality a lot. We enable classiﬁer-free guidance [24] by randomly setting the CLIP embeddings to zero (...
[42] and train on random crops of images that are one-fourth the target size. We use only spatial convolutions
in the model (i.e., no attention layers) and at inference time directly apply the model at the target resolution,
observing that it readily generalizes to the higher resolution. We found no beneﬁt from conditioning the upsamplers on the caption, and use unconditional ADMNets [11] with no guidance.
2.2 Prior

While a decoder can invert CLIP image embeddings zi to produce images x, we need a prior model that produceszi from captionsy to enable image generations from text captions. We explore two different model classes for the prior model: • Autoregressive (AR) prior: the CLIP image embeddingzi is converted into a sequence of discrete codes and predicted autoregressively conditioned on the captiony. • Diffusion prior: The continuous vector zi is directly modelled using a Gaussian diffusion model conditioned on the captiony.
In addition to the caption, we can condition the prior on the CLIP text embeddingzt since it is a deterministic

function of the caption. To improve sample quality we also enable sampling using classiﬁer-free guidance for both the AR and diffusion prior, by randomly dropping this text conditioning information 10% of the time during training. To train and sample from the AR prior more efﬁciently, we ﬁrst reduce the dimensionality of the CLIP image embeddingszi by applying Principal Component Analysis (PCA) [37]. In particular, we ﬁnd that the rank of the CLIP representation space is drastically reduced when training CLIP with SAM [15] while slightly improving evaluation metrics. We are able to preserve nearly all of the information2 by retaining only 319 principal components out of the original 1,024. 3 Image Manipulations

Our approach allows us to encode any given image x into a bipartite latent representation (zi,xT ) that is sufﬁcient for the decoder to produce an accurate reconstruction. The latentzi describes the aspects of the image that are recognized by CLIP, while the latentxT encodes all of the residual information necessary for the decoder to reconstruct x. The former is obtained by simply encoding the image with the CLIP image encoder. The latter is obtained by applying DDIM inversion (Appendix F in [ 11]) tox using the decoder, while conditioning onzi. We describe three different kinds of manipulations that are enabled by this bipartite representation.
3.1 Variations

Given an imagex, we can produce related images that share the same essential content but vary in other apects, such as shape and orientation (Figure 3). To do this, we apply the decoder to the bipartite represen-
tation (zi,xT ) using DDIM withη >0 for sampling. Withη = 0, the decoder becomes deterministic and
will reconstruct the given imagex. Larger values ofη introduce stochasticity into successive sampling steps,

resulting in variations that are perceptually “centered” around the original image x. As η increases, these variations tell us what information was captured in the CLIP image embedding (and thus is preserved across samples), and what was lost (and thus changes across the samples). 6

4 Probing the CLIP Latent Space

Our decoder model provides a unique opportunity to explore CLIP latent space by allowing us to directly visualize what the CLIP image encoder is seeing. As an example use case, we can revisit cases where CLIP makes incorrect predictions, such as typographic attacks [20]. In these adversarial images, a piece of text is overlayed on top of an object, which causes CLIP to predict the object described by the text rather than the object depicted in the image. This piece of text essentially hides the original object in terms of output probabilities. In Figure 6, we show an example of this attack from [20], wherein an apple can be misclassiﬁed as an iPod. Surprisingly, we ﬁnd that our decoder still generates pictures of apples with high probability even though the predicted probability of “Granny Smith” is near zero. Even more notable, the model never produces pictures of iPods, despite the very high relative predicted probability of this caption. 8

6 Related Work

Synthetic image generation is a well studied problem, and most popular techniques for unconditional image generation have also been applied to the text-conditional setting. Many previous works have trained GANs [21] on publicly available image captioning datasets to produce text-conditional image samples [ 56, 63, 49, 58, 57]. Other works have adapted the VQ-V AE approach [52] to text-conditional image generation by training autoregressive transformers on sequences of text tokens followed by image tokens [40, 12, 1]. Finally, some works have applied diffusion models to the problem, training either continuous [35] or discrete [22] diffusion models with auxiliary text encoders to handle textual input. Previous works have leveraged hierarchical generative processes to create high-quality synthetic images. Razavi et al. 7 Limitations and Risks

Although conditioning image generation on CLIP embeddings improves diversity, this choice does come with certain limitations. In particular, unCLIP is worse at binding attributes to objects than a corresponding GLIDE model. In Figure 14, we ﬁnd that unCLIP struggles more than GLIDE with a prompt where it must bind two separate objects (cubes) to two separate attributes (colors). We hypothesize that this occurs because the CLIP embedding itself does not explicitly bind attributes to objects, and ﬁnd that reconstructions from the decoder often mix up attributes and objects, as shown in Figure 15. C Training Details The unCLIP models used for the experiments in this paper were trained with the hyperparameters described below, unless otherwise noted. We additionally trained a production version of unCLIP using similarly sized models but with modiﬁed architectures and trained for longer; we include changes to accommodate
product and safety requirements (e.g. inpainting, preventing unwanted memorization), and train on a larger

dataset that is ﬁltered for aesthetic quality and safety. We report model and training hyperparameters for the paper models in Table 3. All models were trained using Adam [ 27] with corrected weight decay [29] and momentumβ1 = 0.9. Our CLIP model uses a ViT-H/16 [ 13] image encoder that consumes 256× 256 resolution images, and has width 1280 with 32 Transformer [53] blocks. The text encoder also follows the architecture described in Radford et al. [39]: it is a Transformer [53] with a causal attention mask, with width 1024 and 24 Trans-
former blocks. Both models are trained with learning rate 3× 10−4 and SAM [15] withρ = 0.1, where the

perturbations are applied independently by the replicas, each of which uses batch size 64. The remaining hyperparameters are the same as those reported in Radford et al. [39]. When training the encoder, we sample from the CLIP [ 39] and DALL-E [ 40] datasets (approximately 650M images in total) with equal probability. When training the decoder, upsamplers, and prior, we use only the DALL-E dataset [40] (approximately 250M images). Incorporating the noisier CLIP dataset while training the generative stack negatively impacted sample quality in our initial evaluations. Our decoder architecture is the 3.5 billion parameter GLIDE model, with the same architecture and diffusion hyperparameters as in Nichol et al. [35]. We train with learned sigma and sample with 250 strided sampling steps as in Nichol and Dhariwal [34]. We use the ADMNet architecture [11] for the upsamplers. For the AR prior, we use a Transformer text encoder with width 2048 and 24 blocks and a decoder with a causal attention mask, width 1664, and 24 blocks.
